findings.evidence:
The Stripe client is deleted and replaced by the Paylane client in the same
release. There is no switch between the two: keeping both would double the
code to maintain. The Stripe account is closed the day after the release.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: All traffic moves at deploy
findings.recommendation: Keep a way back for the provider switch-over. If Paylane rejects or fails payments after the release, redeploying the previous version cannot help: the Stripe client is gone from the new release and, from the day after, the Stripe account it would call is closed, so checkout stays down until a fix ships (deploys are about weekly). Keep the Stripe client behind a configuration switch (provider per environment) for at least one release cycle, and close the Stripe account only once Paylane has run in production without incident for an agreed period; state the rollback procedure in the design.
findings.title: The Paylane switch-over has no way back

findings.evidence:
A new worker, `settlement-worker`, runs at 02:00, fetches the day's Paylane
payments and matches them to orders. It runs as a Kubernetes CronJob and
writes its result to the database.
findings.location: design.md#Decision: A worker settles payments nightly
findings.recommendation: Decide how a failed or missing run is seen. If the 02:00 CronJob crashes, times out against the Paylane API or is never scheduled, nothing in the design reports it: the only alert (spec "A payment without order") fires from a run that succeeded, so a night with no settlement looks the same as a night with nothing unmatched, and unreconciled payments pile up unnoticed. Add to the design an alert on a failed Job and on the absence of a successful run in the last 24 hours (e.g. a last-success timestamp or metric), plus a structured start/end log with the counts of payments fetched, matched and unmatched.
findings.title: Nobody sees the settlement worker fail
